Retail Workers’ Walkout Shuts Hundreds of Stores Across Japan

TOKYO, June 12 — Thousands of retail workers walked off the job across Japan on Wednesday, forcing the closure of hundreds of stores in a rare show of industrial action in the country’s retail sector. The strike, called by the National Retail Union, began at 8 a.m. local time after overnight talks with employers broke down without agreement on pay and working conditions.

Major chains including Maruya Department Store, FreshMart Supermarkets and Sakura HomeGoods confirmed the closure of multiple outlets, with lines of locked shutters visible in shopping districts from Sapporo to Fukuoka. The National Retail Union said more than 28,000 employees had joined the walkout, marking the largest coordinated action in the sector in over two decades.

“We were left with no other option after management refused to address chronic understaffing and low wages,” union leader Keiko Watanabe told reporters outside the shuttered Maruya flagship store in central Tokyo. “Our members want to return to work, but we need a fair deal.”

Retail companies reported that affected sites included department stores, supermarkets, and home goods outlets. Sakura HomeGoods said 42 of its 60 locations had suspended operations, while FreshMart reported all Tokyo metropolitan area branches were closed for the day. Several 24-hour stores posted notices apologizing and directing customers to check company websites for updates.

Industry analysts said the walkout’s immediate impact was visible in deserted shopping arcades and empty storefronts in urban centers. “This is a significant disruption to day-to-day retail activity,” said retail analyst Daisuke Mori. “It underscores the growing frustration among workers over stagnant pay and heavier workloads.”

Retail Japan, an industry trade association, estimated that up to 35% of the country’s retail workforce was participating in the strike at its peak on Wednesday afternoon. The association called for both parties to resume negotiations. “We urge union representatives and company management to find common ground quickly for the sake of employees and customers alike,” said Retail Japan spokesperson Yutaka Suzuki.

At the time of writing, talks between union officials and management representatives had not resumed. Union leaders indicated the strike would continue into Thursday if no progress was made. Some companies said they were preparing contingency plans, but acknowledged that many outlets could remain closed for a second day.

“We are deeply concerned about the impact on our staff and our customers,” said a Maruya spokesperson. “We hope to resolve this matter as soon as possible.”
